title: Invited to the Reagan-Gorbachev summit in Moscow
summary: Glasnost, the guest list and the stifling curtained room where he was to play.

story.theme_name: Still working: current gigs, upcoming projects and plans

blocks.x: Dave, I want to return to the theme of you being a real ambassador during your career. You were part of the Reagan-Gorbachev summit, and you contributed to creating some lasting goodwill on that occasion. Could you tell me what your recollections are?

With Gorbachev and Reagan. I had a few things come to mind: a room where Garbechev had just made life a lot easier for poets and musicians or political people that had been sent to Siberia. Sitting next to Iola was a general in the Russian Army. Here these people – I wish I could remember the scientist’s name. Or the wife. He was such an important scientist, but he’d been ostracized.
Was that it Iola? Say that again.
She was there. I don’t remember meeting him, but maybe he was. Someplace I have a guest list for this.
Anyway, there’s starting to be a feeling of . . .

. . . glasnost, and yet the United States, I’ve heard, had a list of people that they would send, and I was on the top of the list. They had a list in Russia of people they would accept, and I was on the top of the list. So it was natural that I would go.

Part of that, Dave – excuse me – was also because you’d been there the year before on a cultural exchange. So the Russian people really knew who he was. Then Nancy Reagan was the one, I think, who made a decision that for the state dinner, they would invite you to go.
In this room where we were meeting, floor to ceiling thick curtains were on every window. There was no air in there to speak of, and how many hundred people?
There was a lot crowded into one room, and it was very hot, because it was in May and it was not an air-conditioned room. But obviously there were reasons for keeping that so curtained.
